verifications.note: Fixed on candidate e6979e12 (source 485e91f). packages/db/migrations/0009_business_unit_hierarchy_guard.sql:38-92 adds an AFTER INSERT OR UPDATE OF parent_business_unit_id, organization_id row trigger. It takes pg_advisory_xact_lock(730219, hashtext(organization_id)) and walks the parent chain with SELECT ... FOR SHARE, raising 23514 business_unit_acyclic / business_unit_max_depth. apps/api/src/modules/organization/routes.ts:364 takes the same lock (repository.ts:80-84) BEFORE the FOR UPDATE read and the friendly checks, and :424 maps a trigger refusal to the existing 422 problems. A composite FK (0001:86-87) already rules out cross-organization parents, so a per-organization lock key is sufficient. Re-ran my round-1 repro UNCHANGED (repro-bu/round1-repro-rerun.log): SEC-1 no longer reaches its vulnerable outcome; it times out waiting for a row-lock waiter because the second PATCH now queues on the hierarchy advisory lock. My adversarial round-2 repro (repro-bu/zz-review-r2-bu.test.ts, 7/7 PASS in repro-r2-bu.log) results: (R2-1) the exact round-1 API interleaving gives A->C 200 and B->A 422 business_unit.cycle, with 0 cycles in business_unit_closure; (R2-2) the sequential friendly 422 still holds; (R2-3) direct SQL as mth_app at READ COMMITTED with no API lock gives the loser 23514 business_unit_acyclic; (R2-4) at REPEATABLE READ with the snapshot taken before the winner commits, the loser gets 40001 from the guard's FOR SHARE walk; (R2-5) one multi-row UPDATE putting two roots under each other gives 23514; (R2-6) mth_app cannot SET session_replication_role, ALTER TABLE ... DISABLE TRIGGER or replace the function (42501 x3). The attempt-1 log is kept: my harness waited only for advisory waiters, but at DB level the loser queues on the winner's FOR SHARE row lock. That was a harness fault, not a product fault; the unhandled 40001 in that log already showed fail-closed behaviour. The new bu-hierarchy-guard.test.ts (7) and migrate.test.ts (9 migrations) pass in both integration runs. Residuals (not findings): the REPEATABLE READ depth-only residual is stated in the migration header; a direct-SQL writer that interleaves a row lock with the trigger can hit 40P01, which fails closed.

This runs before the cycle/depth checks; the moved unit is still authorized at :359. Re-ran my round-1 repro UNCHANGED (repro-bu/round1-repro-rerun.log). SEC-2 no longer reaches its vulnerable outcome: the a1-scoped manager's move of a1x under sibling a2 is 403, the a2 auditor still reads 404, and the vulnerable expectation 'expected 403 to be 200' fails. Round-2 repro R2-7 (repro-r2-bu.log): sibling a2 403 forbidden with exactly 1 authorization.denied audit row on a2 ('requires business_unit.manage'); a unit deeper in the sibling branch 403; top level 403; parent unchanged (still a1, version 1); the a2 auditor still 404; the legitimate in-scope move under a1x 200. Fixed. apps/api/src/server.ts keyGenerator returns u:<userId> only when RateLimitSubjects.subjectOf(token) finds the token. Only the identity hook fills that map, after resolveSession succeeds (identity/routes.ts remember/forget). Otherwise it returns ip:<request.ip>; Fastify derives the IP and applies TRUST_PROXY. rate-limit-subjects.ts keys entries by SHA-256 of the token, bounds them (50,000, oldest evicted) with a TTL equal to the idle timeout, and forgets a token on failed resolution, logout or rotation. Re-ran my round-1 repro UNCHANGED (repro-ratelimit/zz-review-ratelimit.log): the bypass test now sees {"429":50}, so its 'never 429' expectation fails. Round-2 repro (zz-review-r2-ratelimit.log, 4/4 PASS, RATE_LIMIT_PER_MINUTE=3): RL-1 a fresh random cookie per request from one IP gives 401,401,401 then 429 x17; RL-2 rotating X-Forwarded-For without TRUST_PROXY still gives 429 from the 4th request; RL-3 two sessions of one user from two IPs share one u: bucket (the 4th request is 429); RL-4 a fake-cookie flood that exhausts an IP's bucket does not starve a valid session from that IP (200); RL-5 a logged-out cookie falls back to the IP bucket (401 x3, then 429).
